rows.verified: Employers must protect workers from health risks arising from regular use of display screen equipment such as computers, laptops, tablets and smartphones.
The Display Screen Equipment Regulations apply to workers who use DSE daily for continuous periods of one hour or more.
Employers must carry out a DSE workstation assessment for workers who meet the definition of a DSE user.
Employers must reduce identified DSE risks, including by arranging breaks from screen work or changes of activity.
Employers must arrange an eye test for a DSE user who asks for one.
Employers must provide glasses where an employee needs them solely for DSE work.
DSE training should cover good posture, furniture adjustment, desk arrangement, glare, breaks, assessments and problem reporting.
For home or hybrid workers, relevant DSE assessments should cover each work setting and workers may self-assess if suitably trained.
DSE risk depends on workstation design, equipment, posture, task duration, break pattern, lighting, training and individual factors.
HSE DSE evidence is worker-, workstation-, task-, environment-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
Employers must manage health and safety risks before people are permitted to work alone.
Lone-working duties apply to contracted workers and may also apply to self-employed people engaged by an organisation.
Employers must train, supervise and monitor lone workers.
Employers must keep in touch with lone workers and have arrangements to respond to incidents.
Risk assessment should consider violence, stress and wellbeing, medical suitability and isolated or rural workplaces.
Certain high-risk work, including some confined-space, live-electrical, diving, explosive-vehicle and fumigation work, requires at least one other person.
Supervision levels should reflect the risk and the worker's ability to identify and handle health and safety issues.
Monitoring, alarm and emergency-contact systems should be understood by workers and tested regularly.
Lone-worker risk depends on the task, location, supervision, communication, violence exposure, medical suitability, emergency response and worker competence.
HSE lone-working evidence is worker-, task-, workplace-, supervision-, communication- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
